q: Is MBRL-1077 actually E. bugandensis, or does the 95.26–95.58% ANI edge case dissolve under modern species-delineation methods?
basis: Paper reports ANI 95.26% AND dDDH 63.9% for MBRL-1077 vs ISS strains. The modern consensus is ANI ≥95% AND dDDH ≥70%; MBRL-1077 clears the ANI cutoff but fails dDDH. Our FastANI rerun lands at 95.53–95.58% (still >95%, but marginal). The paper's SNP tree (Fig.2) also shows MBRL-1077 branching distinctly from the ISS+EB247T+153_ECLO clade. This is an internal inconsistency in the paper, reinforced by our replication.
next_steps: Run pyani-blastn ANI + GGDC 3.0 dDDH between MBRL-1077 and (i) the ISS consensus, (ii) EB-247T, (iii) other Enterobacter type strains from LPSN. Cross-check with core-genome MLST (chewBBACA) and a skani run. If any two of the four modern methods put MBRL-1077 outside E. bugandensis, the paper's C8 story ('MBRL-1077 is a bugandensis carbapenemase producer') should be reframed as 'a related-species carbapenemase producer', changing the epidemiological narrative.

q: Are the five ISS isolates truly independent colonization events, or one event that clonally expanded and was re-sampled five times?
basis: Within-ISS ANI is 99.99–100%. The paper reports 9/12/15/13/… filtered SNPs after GATK HaplotypeCaller (Table S1) but does not test whether that SNP count is consistent with independent colonization vs clonal expansion. Sample geometry (4 from WHC, 1 from ARED, same March-2015 window) is compatible with either scenario; the epidemiology has downstream implications for planetary-protection risk models.
next_steps: Map Illumina reads of all five ISS isolates against IF3SW-P2 as reference with bwa-mem2 + bcftools; enumerate strict SNPs (Q30, DP>10) outside repeats/MGEs. Compare with molecular-clock estimate at ~1e-7 substitutions/site/generation: does observed pairwise SNP distance support a common source <12 months prior to sampling, or centuries? If SNPs cluster along a phylogenetic tree consistent with a single founder + few generations, the 'five independent colonizations' framing is wrong.

q: Does the ISS E. bugandensis actually carry a functional MAR operon (marA/B/C/R), or does the paper's C7 claim rest on annotation heuristics that a modern targeted BLAST would revise?
basis: Our AMRFinderPlus screen does not call marA/B/C/R (out of tool scope; it targets acquired AMR, not chromosomal regulators). The paper's C7 came from RAST subsystem annotation, which is heuristic and often calls marRAB on any MarR-family regulator hit without checking operon structure. This claim is one of the paper's key clinical hooks but was never verified at the level of intact operon integrity.
next_steps: BLASTn the intact E. coli K12 MG1655 marRAB operon (nucleotides + ±200bp flanks) against all eight assemblies. Confirm (i) all four ORFs present in correct order, (ii) intact ribosome binding sites, (iii) intact MarA-box promoter, (iv) no truncating indels. If any of (i)-(iv) fails, downgrade paper's 'functional MAR operon' framing to 'a MarR-family regulator homolog'. Additionally: express marA homolog in E. coli ΔmarRAB background and assay for the paper's predicted efflux upregulation phenotype.

q: Does an independent 2026-era PathogenFinder actually agree with the paper's >79% pathogenicity claim, and is that number meaningful given the reference set has grown ~30× since 2018?
basis: The paper's entire 'crew health consideration' framing pivots on PathogenFinder >79%. We did not re-run PathogenFinder. Between 2018 and 2026 the PathogenFinder reference (both human and animal pathogens) has grown enormously and the tool has been reimplemented (v1 web → v2 CLI). A modern re-score could easily land above OR below 79%, and either outcome is scientifically interesting.
next_steps: Install PathogenFinder v2 (DTU CGE), score all eight assemblies, and compare with the paper's five ISS values. Also cross-check with VirulenceFinder + VFDB BLAST on the same eight assemblies; if the two tools disagree, the paper's confidence number is not portable and the clinical framing should be rewritten around a range, not a single point estimate. Report the delta as 'published 2018 79% → 2026 X%' and treat that delta as itself a data point about how pathogenicity-prediction ML tools age.

q: Do the RefSeq assemblies we (and any 2026+ reader) download match, byte for byte, the assemblies the paper used, or has NCBI silently re-scaffolded them since 2018?
basis: We resolved paper accessions to RefSeq via WGS master ID / strain name; in one case (EB-247T FYBI → GCF_900324475.1) via a strain-name inference. RefSeq re-scaffolds and re-annotates on its own schedule; there is no publicly documented equivalence between the paper's original submissions and the current GCF accessions. If the sequence changed even at contig-boundary level, the paper's ANI/dDDH numbers depend on genome pieces that no longer exist under the same names — a general concern with all WGS papers, but here on the critical path.
next_steps: Pull the WGS-original GenBank submissions from ENA/NCBI at their 2018 snapshot (INSDC keeps versioned records), rerun FastANI on those against our GCF downloads, and quantify sequence-level drift (Δbp, Δcontigs, ΔN50). Publish a small manifest (assembly_map.tsv) mapping 'paper accession' → '2018 submission SHA256' → '2026 GCF SHA256'. If drift is non-zero in any of the eight, add a warning table to REPORT.tex and re-render the ANI matrix on 2018-frozen assemblies for a true apples-to-apples reproduction of Table 1.
